jobs:

      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.x"

      - name: Cache Python packages
        uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: ~/.cache/pip
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-pip-${{ hashFiles('**/requirements.txt') }}
          restore-keys: |
            ${{ runner.os }}-pip-

      - name: Install MkDocs dependencies
        run: |
          pip install --upgrade pip
          pip install mkdocs-material
          pip install "mkdocstrings[python]"
          pip install pillow cairosvg
      - name: Build MkDocs site
        run: mkdocs build        
      - name: Deploy mkdocs
        run: mkdocs gh-deploy --force

mkdocs serve

title: Intro to Streamlit
text:
File Structure
The frontend is organized as follows:
app/front/
├── main.py
├── bandit_utils.py
├── Dockerfile
├── pyproject.toml
├── README.md
├── uv.lock
└── pages/
    ├── 1_Create_Carousels.py
    ├── 2_Interaction.py
    └── 3_Analytics.py
This structure keeps the code modular and easier to maintain.
The idea is simple:

main.py is the Streamlit entry point
pages/ stores each page of the app
bandit_utils.py stores shared logic used across pages
the remaining files support environment, packaging, and deployment

title: Intro to Streamlit
text:
Explanation of Each File

main.py
This is the main entry point of the Streamlit app.
Its job is to:

start the application,
define the landing page,
and let Streamlit automatically discover the files inside the pages/ folder.

In Streamlit, once the pages/ folder exists, each file inside it becomes a separate page in the application.


bandit_utils.py
This file contains the reusable logic shared across all pages.
It is responsible for operations such as:

initializing app state,
creating carousel objects,
sampling visible alternatives,
retrieving carousel statistics,
updating rewards after feedback,
building summary tables,
selecting the active carousel,
identifying the champion bandit,
preparing posterior distribution points for visualization.

This keeps the UI code cleaner because the logic is not repeated inside each page.


pages/1_Create_Carousels.py
This page is responsible for the setup and management of carousel projects.
It allows the user to:

create a new carousel,
define the total number of alternatives,
define how many alternatives are visible at each round,
list existing carousels,
inspect alternatives,
reset a selected carousel,
and prepare the project for interaction.



pages/2_Interaction.py
This page is the live interaction layer of the product.
It allows the user to:

choose a carousel,
see the visible alternatives,
click on one of the shown alternatives,
move to the next round with no click,
or resample the visible set without updating.

This is the page where the Bayesian bandit behavior becomes interactive.


pages/3_Analytics.py
This page is the reporting and visualization layer.
It shows:

total impressions,
total clicks,
average reward,
champion bandit,
posterior mean comparison,
click comparison,
Beta posterior distributions,
detailed result tables,
cumulative reward over time.

This page helps users interpret the results of the carousel experiment.


Supporting Files
The remaining files are used for project setup and packaging:

Dockerfile — container setup for deployment
pyproject.toml — project dependencies and metadata
uv.lock — locked dependency versions when using uv
README.md — project documentation

FROM python:3.12-slim

WORKDIR /app

# Copy pyproject.toml
COPY pyproject.toml .

# Install dependencies
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -e .

# Copy app code
COPY . .

# Expose port
EXPOSE 8501

# Run the app
CMD ["streamlit", "run", "main.py", "--server.port", "8501", "--server.address", "0.0.0.0"]

title: Intro to Streamlit
text:
Step-by-Step Component Development
The frontend can be understood as being developed in stages.

Step 1 | Create the basic Streamlit app
The first step is to create a minimal Streamlit application with:

a main.py file,
a pages/ folder,
and one test page.

The goal here is simply to make sure the app runs and multi-page navigation works.


Step 2 | Build the Create Carousels page
The next step is to build the setup page.
This page is important because it defines the core user input:

project name,
total alternatives,
visible area size.

This is where the app starts to become a product instead of just a demo.


Step 3 | Add shared logic in bandit_utils.py
Once the first page works, common logic should be moved into bandit_utils.py.
This makes the application cleaner because reusable functions such as:

init_state,
create_carousel,
sample_carousel,
get_stats_df,
select_carousel_widget

can be imported by multiple pages.


Step 4 | Build the Interaction page
After the carousel creation flow is ready, the next step is to build the live interaction page.
This page needs to:

display the currently selected bandits,
show current metrics,
record click and no-click events,
update posterior values,
move the carousel to the next round.

This is the core dynamic component of the frontend.


Step 5 | Build the Analytics page
Once interactions are recorded, the next step is to add visualization.
The analytics page should begin with simple outputs such as:

total clicks,
total impressions,
CTR,
posterior mean.

Then it can be extended with richer visuals such as:

champion bandit highlighting,
Beta posterior curves,
cumulative reward over time.



Step 6 | Improve UI and readability
After the basic functionality works, the interface should be improved by:

using better titles and captions,
adding metrics,
organizing results with columns,
improving button labels,
and making the pages more visually clear.



Step 7 | Add placeholders for future backend integration
Even in the MVP stage, it is useful to think ahead.
For example:

delete buttons can be placeholders,
state management can later move to the backend,
page actions can later be replaced with API calls.

This makes the transition to the full product easier.





flowchart LR
    A[Create Carousels] --> B[Shared Logic]
    B --> C[Interaction]
    C --> D[Analytics]
    D --> E[Backend Integration]

Generate Personal Access Token (PAT)
GitHub no longer accepts passwords for Git operations.
You must generate a Personal Access Token (PAT).

Steps

Sign in to your GitHub account.
Navigate to:
Profile → Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Tokens (classic)



Click Generate new token. 
Select scopes (minimum recommended):

repo
read:org
workflow
or simply select all




Set No expiration.



Click Generate token.
Copy the token and store it securely.


You will paste this token when executing:
git push

ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "your_email@example.com"


When prompted for a location, press ENTER to use the default:

~/.ssh/id_rsa

leave empty for no passphrase

or enter a secure passphrase

cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub

macOS:
pbcopy < ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub

Get-Content ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub | Set-Clipboard

Click New SSH key
Paste your key
Save

title: Introduction to Git
text:
Branching for Product Development
Use Git to develop a data product in small, reviewable changes. The same workflow works when you are learning independently or collaborating with others.

Keep the Branch Structure Simple

main contains the stable, working version of the application.
Create a short-lived feature branch for a specific improvement.
Merge the change after checking that it works, then start the next feature from the updated main.

The examples below use main. If your repository uses master, substitute that name in the commands.


Organize Branches Around Changes
A branch describes a change rather than a permanent developer role. For example:

feature/carousel-schema
feature/carousel-api
feature/analytics-page
feature/bandit-evaluation

The database, backend, frontend, and analytical logic still depend on one another. Plan their interfaces and implement them in useful increments; they do not need separate permanent branches.


Example Branch Flow





gitGraph
    commit id: "working MVP"
    branch feature-analytics
    checkout feature-analytics
    commit id: "add performance chart"
    commit id: "check chart behavior"
    checkout main
    merge feature-analytics id: "merge checked feature"

title: Introduction to Git
text:
Step-by-Step Feature Workflow

1. Open the Repository
If you have not cloned it yet:
git clone https://github.com/your-username/your-repo.git
cd your-repo
Otherwise, open your existing local repository.


2. Update the Stable Branch
git checkout main
git pull --ff-only origin main


3. Create a Feature Branch
git checkout -b feature/analytics-page


4. Implement and Check the Change
Make a focused improvement, such as adding a chart to the analytics page. Run the relevant part of the application and check the result against the intended user behavior.
Review the files before committing:
git status
git diff


5. Commit and Push
Stage the files you changed. For example, if you updated the analytics page:
git add app/front/pages/Analytics.py
git commit -m "Add carousel performance chart"
git push -u origin feature/analytics-page


6. Review and Merge
A Pull Request (PR) on GitHub lets you inspect the difference between the feature branch and main, describe the change, and keep a record of the review.
When working independently, you can review and merge your own PR after checking the behavior. When collaborating, a PR also provides a place to ask for feedback.

title: Introduction to Git
text:
Pull Requests

Why Pull Requests Matter
Pull Requests help you:

review the changes before merging,
explain what changed and why,
record how you checked the result,
discuss implementation choices when feedback is useful,
keep main working.



Pull Request Steps on GitHub
After pushing your feature branch:

Open the repository on GitHub.
Click Compare & pull request.
Set base to main and compare to your feature branch.
Add a clear title and describe the product behavior that changed.
Include how you checked it and any known limitations.
Review the diff and address any feedback.
Merge when the change is ready.

For example: feature/analytics-page → main.


Continue from the Updated Version
After the PR is merged:
git checkout main
git pull --ff-only origin main
Create a new feature branch from this version for the next improvement.

title: Introduction to Git
text:
Merge Conflicts
A merge conflict happens when Git cannot automatically combine changes from two branches.






Important



This usually happens when:

two people edit the same file
two people edit the same lines in a file
one person deletes something that another person modified




Example Conflict Situation
Suppose:

One feature branch changes bandit_utils.py
Another feature branch changes the same part of bandit_utils.py

When one branch is merged first, the second branch may conflict.





gitGraph
    commit id: "base"
    
    branch feature-a
    checkout feature-a
    commit id: "change A"
    
    checkout main
    branch feature-b
    checkout feature-b
    commit id: "change B"








What a conflict looks like
Git may mark the file like this:
<<<<<<< HEAD
return {"message": "First implementation"}
=======
return {"message": "Alternative implementation"}
>>>>>>> feature-branch

This means Git needs a human to decide which version to keep.



How to resolve a merge conflict

Pull the latest changes from the target branch.
Open the conflicted file.
Find the conflict markers:

<<<<<<<
=======
>>>>>>>

Decide which code should remain.
Remove the conflict markers.
Save the file.
Stage and commit the resolved version.

Example:
git add .
git commit -m "Resolve merge conflict"
git push


Best ways to avoid conflicts
To reduce merge conflicts:

pull frequently
keep branches focused and small
do not let branches drift for too long
communicate who is editing which files
use Pull Requests early
avoid editing the same file in parallel unless necessary

title: Introduction to Git
text:
Recommended Development Process

Choose a small improvement linked to the user’s needs.
Update main and create a feature branch.
Implement the change locally.
Check the behavior and review the diff.
Commit, push, and open a Pull Request.
Review and merge the working change.
Pull the updated main before starting the next improvement.

title: Product
text:
We will start with the general process: define a useful product, choose its MVP, prioritize the work, and connect the components. The diagrams below support each step. Then we will apply the process to the Bayesian Carousel Bandits example.









flowchart LR
    accTitle: The product-building cycle
    accDescr: Define a user problem, choose a small MVP, build it, observe use, and improve it using feedback.
    P["Understand the<br/>user's problem"] --> M["Choose a<br/>small MVP"]
    M --> B["Build a<br/>usable version"]
    B --> T["Let users try it<br/>and measure results"]
    T --> I["Choose the<br/>next improvement"]
    I --> M






Read the diagram from left to right. Start with a decision the user needs to make, choose the smallest useful solution, and build something they can try. Observe what happens and use the results to choose the next version.
For the carousel example, the first useful flow is: create a carousel → show alternatives → record a click → see the results. Later versions can add richer analytics and more deployment options.



Before choosing tools or building a model, answer:

Who is the user? Identify who will use the result.
What decision do they need to make? Describe the problem in practical terms.
How will the product help? Define the action or insight it should provide.
How will we measure success? Choose a metric linked to the user’s goal.

For example, a marketer needs to choose which offers to display in a carousel. The product uses click feedback to update its selection and reports metrics such as click-through rate and cumulative reward.



The Minimum Viable Product (MVP) is the smallest usable version that lets us try the core idea and learn from feedback.

Choose one clear user flow.
Include only the features needed to complete that flow.
Make the result visible and easy to try.
Use feedback and measured results to decide what to improve next.

Keep quality consistent across the core user flow so the complete experience is usable.



An unevenly developed MVP illustrates why the whole user experience needs attention





Separate features into Must have, Should have, Could have, and Won’t have for now. Keep the first version focused on the must-have features.



MoSCoW prioritization board: Must Have, Should Have, Could Have, and Won’t Have





Describe what the user does from start to finish. Build a low-fidelity mockup to check that the inputs, actions, and results make sense before implementing the interface.
Tools such as Stitch and Figma can help turn the idea into a mockup.



Each iteration should let the user do something useful. Start with a working prototype and add complexity when it supports the product’s purpose.
The lower sequence delivers a usable way to travel at every stage. Apply the same idea to a data product: each version should complete a useful user flow.



MVP development from a skateboard to a car, delivering a usable product at each stage


Let someone try the MVP, observe where they struggle, and compare the results with the success metric. Use that feedback to choose the next improvement.






Use a roadmap to describe how the product can grow:

Define the problem, user, and success metric.
Sketch the user flow and choose the MVP scope.
Prepare data and prototype the analytical logic.
Build an interactive prototype that demonstrates the core value.
Add persistent storage and connect the interface and backend.
Try the complete flow, collect feedback, and improve it.
Document setup, usage, and limitations.

A roadmap describes the intended sequence. Adjust it as you learn from the data, implementation, and user feedback.
Use the diagram below to discuss dependencies between frontend, backend, and analytical work. Each block represents a piece of functionality, and the arrows show what needs to be ready before the next piece can be completed.



Example product roadmap with dependencies across frontend, backend, and data science work





Break each step into small tasks with an observable result, such as creating a carousel, recording a click, or displaying a performance chart.
Track progress with a simple flow:
\[\text{Backlog} \rightarrow \text{In Progress} \rightarrow \text{Review} \rightarrow \text{Done}\]

Backlog: describe the change and what successful completion looks like.
In Progress: implement a focused change and record any blockers.
Review: check the behavior against the task and the user’s needs.
Done: the change works and the relevant documentation is updated.

A task board such as GitHub Projects can help organize this work.




We will cover each component and practice connecting it to the rest of the application.


These are three parts of the application with different jobs. In the architecture we will build, they work together to turn a user’s action into a useful result.








Part
In simple terms
In our carousel product




Frontend — Streamlit
The interface people use: pages, buttons, forms, and charts.
A marketer creates a carousel and opens its analytics page.


Backend — FastAPI
The service that receives requests, applies the rules, and returns results.
It validates carousel settings, runs analytical logic, and prepares analytics results.


Database — PostgreSQL
Organized, lasting storage that the application can read and update.
It stores carousels, alternatives, clicks, and interaction history.






An API is an agreed way for one program to request something from another. For example, the frontend can ask the backend to return the results for a selected carousel.





flowchart LR
    accTitle: How the user, frontend, backend, and database connect
    accDescr: The browser interacts with Streamlit. Streamlit sends requests to FastAPI. FastAPI reads or writes PostgreSQL, and the results return along the same path.
    U["User<br/>Browser"] <-->|"actions / screens"| F["Frontend<br/>Streamlit"]
    F <-->|"API requests / results"| B["Backend<br/>FastAPI"]
    B <-->|"queries / records"| D[("Database<br/>PostgreSQL")]
    classDef frontend fill:#e7f1ff,stroke:#2563eb,color:#172554;
    classDef backend fill:#f0eaff,stroke:#7c3aed,color:#3b0764;
    classDef database fill:#e2f5eb,stroke:#15803d,color:#14532d;
    class F frontend;
    class B backend;
    class D database;






Follow one action: opening the analytics page.

The user selects a carousel in the browser.
The frontend asks the backend for that carousel’s analytics through the API.
The backend asks the database for the relevant interactions and prepares the requested metrics.
The database returns the stored records to the backend.
The backend returns the results to the frontend.
The frontend displays the charts and tables to the user.

The arrows go both ways because each request has a response. When recording a click, the backend writes a new interaction to the database before returning a result. The browser reaches the stored data through these application services.






Where does Streamlit run?



The browser displays the interface, while Streamlit’s Python code runs in a server process. In our design, that Python code calls the separate FastAPI service. We call Streamlit the frontend service because it provides the user interface. See Streamlit’s architecture.





The analytical code turns data into a decision or an insight. For our carousel, it selects alternatives and updates beliefs using click feedback. We will develop this logic in Python and make it available through the backend. The frontend explains the result; the database keeps the history needed to produce it.




Identify the data needed to solve the problem.
Collect, generate, clean, and transform data as needed.
Build a repeatable processing pipeline when the application requires it.





Explore the data and choose an appropriate analytical method.
Build and evaluate the analytical logic or model.
Define performance metrics and explain the results and limitations.
Make model outputs available to the application and store results when needed.




Use PostgreSQL to manage the application’s data:

Design the data structure and tables.
Store application settings, interactions, and analytical results.
Create, read, update, and delete records from Python.




Use FastAPI to expose the operations the product needs:

Define endpoints around the user’s actions and the business logic.
Validate inputs and return structured responses.
Connect the interface to the database and analytical logic.
Explain and try endpoints through the API documentation.




Frontend and backend responsibilities in an application





Use Streamlit to build an interface where users can provide input, interact with the analytical logic, and explore results.

Quick prototyping: turn Python scripts into interactive applications.
Interactive controls: use sliders, forms, and buttons to explore different inputs.
Visualizations: present results with charts and tables, using libraries such as Seaborn and Plotly where useful.
Integration: connect the interface to the backend and display its responses.




Use Git to track changes and develop features in small steps. Use Docker and Docker Compose to package services and run them together in a reproducible environment.



Use MkDocs to explain the product’s purpose, setup, usage, architecture, and limitations so someone else can run and understand it.




A service is a running application that owns a responsibility and exposes a way to use it. A microservices architecture divides a product into independently deployable services organized around business capabilities, such as managing experiments or producing recommendations. Services agree on their inputs and outputs through APIs. Microsoft’s architecture guide describes these boundaries.


Our first target is a layered application deployed as several containers: Streamlit presents the interface, FastAPI owns the product operations, and PostgreSQL stores the records. The bandit calculation can remain a Python module inside FastAPI.





flowchart LR
    accTitle: The first service boundaries for the carousel product
    accDescr: A browser uses the Streamlit service, which calls the FastAPI service. FastAPI contains the bandit logic and accesses PostgreSQL.
    U["Browser"] <-->|"screens and actions"| F["Frontend service<br/>Streamlit"]
    subgraph API["Backend service — FastAPI"]
        R["API routes"] --> L["Product rules<br/>and bandit logic"]
    end
    F <-->|"HTTP and JSON"| R
    L <-->|"SQLAlchemy and SQL"| D[("PostgreSQL")]






Read each box as a responsibility. Streamlit asks for an operation; FastAPI decides what it means and performs it; PostgreSQL keeps the resulting data. Changing the chart layout can stay within the frontend, while changing a database query belongs in the backend’s data-access code.
The current Streamlit MVP still keeps its state locally and contains TODOs for API integration. This diagram is the design we are working toward, rather than a claim that every connection is already implemented.











Term
What it describes
Example




Component
A part of the code or system.
A Python function that samples bandit alternatives.


Service
A separately running application with a defined responsibility.
The FastAPI application listening on port 8000.


Container
The environment in which an application runs.
A container containing Python, FastAPI, and our backend code.


Microservice
A service with a focused business boundary that can be deployed independently.
A future recommendation service with its own API and data ownership.



Putting the frontend, API, and database into three containers gives us a useful deployment structure. A larger microservices design also needs clear ownership, compatible API contracts, and independent release decisions.



Suppose recommendation traffic grows while experiment management changes rarely. A possible future design is:





flowchart TB
    accTitle: A possible future microservices design with separate data ownership
    accDescr: A frontend calls an experiment service and a recommendation service through APIs. Each service owns its own data store, and the recommendation service requests experiment information through the experiment API.
    F["Frontend"] <-->|"create or inspect experiments"| E["Experiment service"]
    F <-->|"request a selection"| R["Recommendation service"]
    E <-->|"owns"| ED[("Experiment data")]
    R <-->|"owns"| RD[("Recommendation state")]
    R -->|"request experiment information by API"| E






Follow the ownership arrows. Each service controls its data and offers an API to other services. Another service asks for information through that API instead of depending directly on its internal tables. The stores could be separate databases on the same database server; the ownership boundary matters more than the number of machines.
This is a future design example. It does not require splitting the learning MVP into extra services. See microservice data ownership.








sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant F as Streamlit
    participant B as FastAPI
    participant D as PostgreSQL
    U->>F: Create a carousel
    F->>B: POST /carousels with JSON settings
    B->>B: Validate settings and prepare records
    B->>D: INSERT carousel and alternatives
    D-->>B: Saved records and identifiers
    B-->>F: HTTP response with JSON
    F-->>U: Show the created carousel






Read this diagram from top to bottom. Each arrow crosses a boundary. The API contract tells the frontend which fields to send and which response to expect. SQLAlchemy helps the backend turn Python objects into database operations.




Separate changes: update the interface while keeping the API contract stable.
Independent deployment: replace a service without rebuilding every other service when their contracts remain compatible.
Focused scaling: run more instances of a busy service when the deployment supports it.
Network failures: a request can time out even when the calling service is healthy; define timeouts and useful error responses.
Data consistency: an operation spanning services may need coordination. Retrying a request that creates something can create duplicates unless the API handles repeated requests deliberately.

For the MVP, use the smallest architecture that delivers the user flow. Add service boundaries when they make responsibilities and deployment easier to manage.




A container runs an application in an isolated environment with the files and libraries it needs. For example, a backend container runs our FastAPI code with Python and the required packages. Containers share their host’s operating-system kernel, which manages processes and hardware resources. Docker’s container guide explains this model.







flowchart LR
    accTitle: From application code to a running container
    accDescr: Application code, dependency definitions, and a Dockerfile are used to build an image. Docker starts a container from that image.
    S["Code + dependencies<br/>+ Dockerfile"] -->|"build"| I["Image<br/>Prepared package"]
    I -->|"run"| C["Container<br/>Running application"]
    classDef package fill:#fff1dc,stroke:#c56a13,color:#713f12;
    class I,C package;







Dockerfile: the build instructions, such as choosing Python, installing packages, and copying our code.
Image: the prepared package used to create a container.
Container: an instance of that image running with its own configuration.

Read the arrows as actions: we build an image, then run a container from it. This makes the application environment repeatable on compatible machines. See Docker’s explanation of images and containers.




The Docker host is the physical or virtual machine where Docker Engine runs and manages containers. Docker Engine is the software that creates, starts, and stops them. Your computer can provide this environment during development; a server can provide it when the product is deployed. See the Docker Engine overview.







flowchart TB
    accTitle: Three application containers on one Docker host
    accDescr: A browser connects to the frontend container on a Docker host. The frontend calls the backend, the backend accesses the database, and database files are stored in a persistent volume. Docker Engine manages the containers.
    U["User's browser"]
    subgraph HOST["Docker host — the machine running Docker Engine"]
        direction TB
        E["Docker Engine<br/>Manages the containers"]
        subgraph NET["Application network — lets the services communicate"]
            direction LR
            F["Frontend container<br/>Streamlit"] <-->|"API"| B["Backend container<br/>FastAPI + analytical code"]
            B <-->|"read / write"| D[("Database container<br/>PostgreSQL")]
        end
        V[("Volume<br/>Saved database files")]
        E -.->|"manages"| F
        E -.->|"manages"| B
        E -.->|"manages"| D
        D <-->|"stores data"| V
    end
    U <-->|"published frontend port"| F
    classDef frontend fill:#e7f1ff,stroke:#2563eb,color:#172554;
    classDef backend fill:#f0eaff,stroke:#7c3aed,color:#3b0764;
    classDef database fill:#e2f5eb,stroke:#15803d,color:#14532d;
    classDef docker fill:#fff1dc,stroke:#c56a13,color:#713f12;
    class F frontend;
    class B backend;
    class D,V database;
    class E docker;






Read the diagram from the outside in. The outer box is the host. Inside it, Docker Engine manages three containers. The solid arrows show application communication; the dotted arrows show management by Docker Engine.

One container per service: the interface, API, and database each have their own running environment.
A network connects them: the frontend can reach the backend, and the backend can reach the database.
A published port lets the browser in: for example, a local address such as http://localhost:8501 can lead to the Streamlit container when that port is published.
A volume keeps database files: the data can survive replacing the database container, as long as the volume is retained. See Docker volumes.

On macOS and Windows, Docker Desktop runs Linux containers in a managed Linux virtual environment. The Docker Engine and Linux containers live there, while you use Docker from your normal desktop. See Docker Desktop networking.



Docker Compose describes the services, their connections, and their storage in one configuration file. It lets us start the product’s containers together. Follow the Docker tutorial to build this setup; the official Compose overview explains the same service, network, and volume concepts.



Start with a usable Streamlit MVP, develop the analytical logic, add persistent storage and API operations, then connect the services. Package the services as containers and run them together. At each step, check that the original user flow still works.






The components work together to move data through the application and make results available to the user.



Data product schema connecting the API, database, model, and data preparation





This architecture shows how the components can fit together as the application grows. An early MVP can start with fewer components; we will explore the full architecture through the tutorials.



Example container architecture connecting the database, data processing, model, API, and Streamlit interface

Read the diagram from the outside in. The outer box is the host. Inside it, Docker Engine manages three containers. The solid arrows show application communication; the dotted arrows show management by Docker Engine.

One container per service: the interface, API, and database each have their own running environment.
A network connects them: the frontend can reach the backend, and the backend can reach the database.
A published port lets the browser in: for example, a local address such as http://localhost:8501 can lead to the Streamlit container when that port is published.
A volume keeps database files: the data can survive replacing the database container, as long as the volume is retained. See Docker volumes.

On macOS and Windows, Docker Desktop runs Linux containers in a managed Linux virtual environment. The Docker Engine and Linux containers live there, while you use Docker from your normal desktop. See Docker Desktop networking.

title: Product
text:
Product Summary
This Bayesian Carousel Optimization application is a guided example of building a Marketing Analytics data product.
The product simulates a real-world marketing problem where a team has multiple creative alternatives, offers, or content items (bandits), but can only show a limited number of them in a visible carousel area at a time.
Instead of randomly choosing which alternatives to display, the system uses Bayesian learning and Thompson Sampling to adaptively prioritize the alternatives that appear to perform better based on observed user clicks.
The MVP is implemented as a multi-page Streamlit app and is designed as the frontend prototype of a larger product that can later be integrated with a backend API, database, and deployment pipeline.

title: Product
text:
Problem Definition

Business Problem
Marketing teams often need to choose among multiple alternatives such as:

promotional banners,
campaign creatives,
product cards,
or recommendation tiles.

However, only a limited number of alternatives can be shown to users at once in a carousel or visible content area.
The key challenge is:

How can we decide which alternatives to show in each round so that we learn from user behavior and gradually improve click performance over time?

A static rule-based system or random selection is inefficient because:

it may keep showing underperforming alternatives,
it does not learn from feedback,
and it does not balance experimentation with optimization.



Specific Problem Statement
We want to build a product that:

creates carousel projects with a configurable number of total alternatives,
chooses only a subset of alternatives to display in the visible area,
collects interaction feedback in the form of clicks / no-clicks,
updates beliefs about each alternative after every round,
and visualizes which alternatives are performing best over time.

This is modeled as a multi-armed bandit problem with:

Bernoulli rewards
Beta priors/posteriors
Thompson Sampling for selection

title: Product
text:
Proposed Solution

Core Idea
Each alternative in a carousel is treated as a bandit arm.
For every alternative, the system keeps:

a prior belief about its click-through rate,
updates that belief after each user interaction,
and samples from the posterior to decide which alternatives should be displayed next.

The visible area might show, for example:

4 visible alternatives out of 10 total alternatives


At every round:

the system samples a score for each alternative from its Beta posterior,
selects the top alternatives according to Thompson Sampling,
displays them in the carousel,
observes a user click or no-click outcome,
updates the posteriors,
and repeats the process.

This allows the system to balance:

exploration of uncertain alternatives,
exploitation of alternatives that already look strong.

title: Product
text:
Current MVP

What We Have Built
The current MVP is a Streamlit application with 3 pages:

Page 1 | Create Carousels
This page allows the user (Page 1 URL):

create a new carousel project,
define the total number of alternatives,
define the visible area size,
list all available carousel projects,
inspect the alternatives of a selected carousel,
reset a selected carousel.




Page 2 | Interaction
This page is where the live bandit interaction happens (Page 2 URL).
The user can:

choose a carousel,
see the currently selected visible alternatives,
click one of the displayed alternatives,
move to the next round with no click,
or resample without updating.

For every round, the app updates:

impressions,
clicks,
alpha / beta values,
posterior mean,
and empirical CTR.




Page 3 | Analytics
This page summarizes performance for each carousel project (Page 3 URL).
It currently includes:

overall carousel project listing,
total impressions,
total clicks,
average reward,
champion bandit identification,
posterior mean comparison,
click comparison,
Beta posterior distribution visualization,
detailed results table,
cumulative reward over time.

title: Product
text:
Methodology

Reward Structure
We use a Bernoulli reward:

1 = user clicked one of the displayed alternatives
0 = no click for a displayed alternative



Bayesian Model
For each alternative, we model click probability using a Beta-Bernoulli setup:

Prior: Beta(alpha, beta)
Outcome: Bernoulli click / no-click
Posterior update:

clicked alternative: alpha += 1
displayed but unclicked alternatives: beta += 1




Selection Strategy
We use Thompson Sampling:

draw one sample from each alternative’s posterior,
rank alternatives by the sampled values,
display the top k alternatives where k = visible_count.




The Value
This product is a strong fit for Marketing Analytics because it demonstrates:

experimentation under uncertainty,
user behavior learning,
adaptive optimization,
measurable reward improvement,
and a clear connection between analytics and product decision-making.


Instead of simply reporting past A/B test results, the system actively decides what to show next based on observed performance.

text:
Steps to Achieve the Full Product

Step 1 | Finalize the MVP logic

validate carousel creation flow,
validate selection and update rules,
confirm reward assumptions,
confirm analytics outputs.



Step 2 | Separate frontend from logic

move bandit logic from Streamlit session state into reusable backend functions,
define clear API contracts,
keep Streamlit as the UI layer only,
learn basic requests with FastAPI



Step 3 | Build backend endpoints
Planned API functionality:

create carousel,
list carousels,
fetch selected visible alternatives,
submit click / no-click feedback,
get analytics for a carousel,
reset or delete a carousel.



Step 4 | Add database persistence
Create PostgreSQL tables for:

carousel projects,
alternatives,
interaction history,
posterior parameters,
analytics summaries.



Step 5 | Connect frontend to backend
Update the Streamlit pages so they:

fetch data from API,
submit interaction events,
display live analytics from the database.



Step 6 | Improve analytics
Extend the analytics layer with:

richer reward history,
posterior distribution comparison,
best-bandit explanation,
possible regret or lift analysis.



Step 7 | Polish product UX

improve visual hierarchy,
improve labeling and explanations,
add screenshots and deployment URL,
add project documentation.



Step 8 | Containerize and deploy

add Docker support,
configure environment variables,
deploy the frontend,
connect deployed frontend to backend and DB.

title: Introduction to Docker
text:
Docker Commands: Predict, Run, Explain
In this lab, each command answers a question about images, containers, or communication. Outputs below are representative and sometimes abbreviated. Versions, IDs, timestamps, progress messages, and column spacing will vary on your machine.
Use a disposable container named tutorial-web for the first exercises. It runs Python’s small HTTP server so we can study Docker before adding our product code. This server is a teaching example, not the carousel backend.





flowchart LR
    accTitle: Docker image and container lifecycle
    accDescr: Pull an image, run a new container, inspect it while running, stop and restart it, and finally remove the stopped container. The downloaded image remains.
    I["Download image<br/>docker pull"] --> R["Create and start<br/>docker run"]
    R --> O["Observe<br/>ps, logs, exec"]
    O --> S["Stop<br/>docker stop"]
    S -->|"docker start"| O
    S --> X["Remove container<br/>docker rm"]






Follow the arrows: an image is the starting package; the container is the instance we create from it. Stopping preserves that instance, starting resumes it, and removing deletes that instance. The image remains available for another run.

1. Can the CLI Reach Docker Engine?
docker version
Expected output, abbreviated:
Client:
 Version: <installed client version>
 ...
Server: Docker Desktop
 Engine:
  Version: <installed engine version>
 ...
The Client is the command-line tool. The Server is Docker Engine, which runs containers. A connection error mentioning docker.sock means the CLI cannot reach the engine; start Docker Desktop and try again. A successful docker --version alone only confirms the CLI is installed.


2. Download an Image
docker pull python:3.12-slim
Expected output, abbreviated:
3.12-slim: Pulling from library/python
...: Pull complete
Digest: sha256:<image digest>
Status: Downloaded newer image for python:3.12-slim
If it is already downloaded and current, the final status can say Image is up to date. No container has been started yet.
docker image ls python
Expected output, abbreviated:
REPOSITORY   TAG         IMAGE ID       ...
python       3.12-slim   <image-id>     ...
This lists the local image package. Compare it with the running-container list in the next step.


3. Start a Container and Publish a Port
docker run --name tutorial-web -d -p 8088:8000 python:3.12-slim python -u -m http.server 8000
Expected output:
<new container ID>

--name tutorial-web gives the instance a memorable name.
-d leaves it running in the background.
-p 8088:8000 forwards host port 8088 to container port 8000.
python:3.12-slim selects the image.
Everything after the image name is the program to run inside the container.

Open http://localhost:8088. You should see a directory listing from the Python HTTP server.





flowchart LR
    accTitle: Host port to container port mapping
    accDescr: A browser requests localhost port 8088. Docker forwards the connection to the Python HTTP server at port 8000 inside tutorial-web.
    B["Browser<br/>localhost:8088"] <-->|"published port"| P["Docker port forwarding<br/>8088 to 8000"]
    P <-->|"HTTP"| C["tutorial-web container<br/>Python server on 8000"]






The two ports can be different. The browser uses the host-side port. The program inside the container keeps listening on its own port. See the Docker run reference.


4. Is It Running?
docker ps --filter name=tutorial-web --format "table {{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}\t{{.Ports}}"
Expected output, abbreviated:
NAMES          STATUS          PORTS
tutorial-web   Up ...          0.0.0.0:8088->8000/tcp ...
Up means the container process is running. It does not by itself prove the application is ready to handle requests. docker ps shows running containers; docker ps -a includes stopped ones. See container listing.


5. Read the Application’s Logs
docker logs tutorial-web
Expected output, abbreviated:
Serving HTTP on 0.0.0.0 port 8000 ...
... "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 -
The request line appears after visiting the page. The 200 is an HTTP success status. Logs are the program’s output, which helps us understand what the application is doing.


6. Run Another Command Inside the Existing Container
docker exec tutorial-web python -c "import sys; print('Python inside container:', sys.version_info.major, sys.version_info.minor)"
Expected output:
Python inside container: 3 12
This uses Python inside the running container. exec starts an additional process in that container; it does not create another container.


7. Stop, Start, and Remove the Practice Container
docker stop tutorial-web
Expected output: tutorial-web.
docker ps -a --filter name=tutorial-web --format "table {{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}"
Expected output, abbreviated:
NAMES          STATUS
tutorial-web   Exited (...) ...
The process has stopped, but the container still exists. Its name and exit information are still available.
docker start tutorial-web
Expected output: tutorial-web. Refresh the browser: the same instance is running again.
Finish this practice exercise with:
docker stop tutorial-web
docker rm tutorial-web
Each command prints tutorial-web. The container is removed; the Python image remains. Keep product data in a volume or bind mount when it must survive replacing a container.


8. Apply the Same Ideas to the Product with Compose
The repository’s Compose file is at app/docker-compose.yaml. From the repository root, enter that directory:
cd app
docker compose --env-file .env config --services
Expected service names, with order allowed to vary:
db
pgadmin
etl
backend
frontend
This checks configuration and lists service names without starting them. The database lesson explains how to create app/.env using placeholder credentials.
For the backend model version of the product, use a database initialized with those models, then start these services:
docker compose up -d --build db backend frontend
Expected output, abbreviated after the image build:
Container postgresql_db_aua   Healthy
Container bandit_backend     Started
Container streamlit_frontend Started
--build rebuilds application images before starting the services; -d keeps them in the background. The backend waits for the database health check. The ETL service uses a different schema version, explained in the database lesson, so it is a separate exercise. See Compose up.








Question
Command from app/
What to expect




Which services are running?
docker compose ps
Service rows with Up or running; the DB can also show healthy.


What is the API doing?
docker compose logs --tail 10 backend
Uvicorn startup messages or useful errors.


Is PostgreSQL ready?
docker compose exec db sh -c 'pg_isready -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB"'
A line ending in accepting connections.


Does the API respond?
curl http://localhost:8000/health
{"status":"ok"} from the repository backend.


How do I stop this Compose application?
docker compose down
Messages showing containers and the application network being removed.



down removes the application’s containers. Our repository’s database files use a bind mount at app/postgres_data, which remains on disk. A named volume is another persistence option; the volume section below explains the distinction.

title: Introduction to Docker
text:
Dockerfile
A Dockerfile is a text file that describes how to build a Docker image.
You can think of it as a recipe for your application environment. It defines: - the base image, - the working directory, - the dependencies, - the files that should be copied, - and the command that starts the application.

Why do we need a Dockerfile?
Instead of saying “it works on my machine”, we define the environment in code so the application can run the same way on different machines and servers.





flowchart LR
    A[Source Code] --> B[Dockerfile]
    B --> C[Docker Image]
    C --> D[Docker Container]
    D --> E[Application Running]








Common Dockerfile Instructions
The most common instructions are:

FROM — defines the base image
WORKDIR — sets the working directory inside the container
COPY — copies files into the container
RUN — executes commands during image build
EXPOSE — documents the application port
CMD — defines the startup command



Example 1 | Simple Python Application
FROM python:3.13-slim

WORKDIR /app

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY . .

CMD ["python", "main.py"]

What happens in this example?
Step by step:

FROM python:3.13-slim starts from a lightweight Python image
WORKDIR /app creates and uses /app as the working directory
COPY requirements.txt . copies the dependency file into the image
RUN pip install ... installs Python packages
COPY . . copies the application code
CMD [...] starts the application when the container runs






flowchart TD
    A[FROM python:3.13-slim] --> B[WORKDIR /app]
    B --> C[COPY requirements.txt]
    C --> D[RUN pip install]
    D --> E[COPY source code]
    E --> F[CMD python main.py]









Example 2 | Streamlit Application
For our frontend, we may use Streamlit. A Dockerfile for the frontend could look like this:
FROM python:3.13-slim

WORKDIR /app

COPY pyproject.toml .
COPY uv.lock .

RUN pip install uv && uv sync

COPY . .

EXPOSE 8501

CMD ["uv", "run", "streamlit", "run", "main.py", "--server.address=0.0.0.0", "--server.port=8501"]


Build the Docker Image
Run the following command in the folder where the Dockerfile is located:
docker build -t my-streamlit-app .


Run the Container
docker run -p 8501:8501 my-streamlit-app
This means:

port 8501 on your machine
is mapped to port 8501 inside the container

title: Introduction to Docker
text:
Docker Compose
Docker Compose is a tool for running multiple containers together using a single configuration file, usually called docker-compose.yml.
This is useful when a project has more than one service, for example:

frontend,
backend,
database
data modeling
etc

Instead of starting every container manually, Docker Compose lets us manage the whole system in one place.





flowchart LR
    A[docker-compose.yml] --> B[Frontend Container]
    A --> C[Backend Container]
    A --> D[PostgreSQL Container]
    B <--> C
    C <--> D







Why do we need Docker Compose?
Without Docker Compose, we would need to start every container manually and configure ports, networking, and environment variables by hand.
With Compose, one command can start the entire application stack:
docker compose up


Basic Structure of a Compose File
A Compose file usually contains:

services — all containers we want to run
build or image — how each service is created
ports — exposed ports
volumes — persistent or shared storage
environment — environment variables
depends_on — startup dependency order



Example 1 | Application and PostgreSQL
services:
  app:
    build: .
    container_name: my_app
    ports:
      - "8501:8501"
    depends_on:
      - db

  db:
    image: postgres:17
    container_name: my_postgres
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: ${DB_NAME}
      POSTGRES_USER: ${DB_USER}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  postgres_data:

What happens in this example?
This file defines two services:

app: the main application container
db: the PostgreSQL database container

The database stores its data in a Docker volume so the data is not lost when the container stops.



Example 2 | Frontend, Backend, and Database
This version shows how a data product can connect a frontend, backend, and database:
services:
  frontend:
    build: ./app/front # I have app folder which contains the whole product
    container_name: frontend
    ports:
      - "8501:8501"
    depends_on:
      - backend

  backend:
    build: ./app/backend
    container_name: backend
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    depends_on:
      - db
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://postgres:postgres@db:5432/project_db

  db:
    image: postgres:17
    container_name: db
    restart: always
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: ${DB_NAME}
      POSTGRES_USER: ${DB_USER}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  postgres_data:





flowchart TD
    U[User] --> F[Frontend :8501]
    F --> B[Backend :8000]
    B --> P[PostgreSQL :5432]








Example 3 | Jupyter Notebook Server
A Jupyter Notebook server can also run inside a container. This is useful for data exploration, EDA, model prototyping, and reproducible environments.
A simple Dockerfile example:
FROM jupyter/base-notebook:latest

WORKDIR /home/jovyan/work

COPY . /home/jovyan/work

EXPOSE 8888

CMD ["start-notebook.sh", "--NotebookApp.token=''", "--NotebookApp.password=''"]

What happens in this example?
Step by step:

FROM jupyter/base-notebook:latest starts from the official Jupyter notebook image
WORKDIR /home/jovyan/work sets the working directory
COPY . /home/jovyan/work copies your notebooks and files into the container
EXPOSE 8888 documents the notebook server port
CMD [...] starts the Jupyter notebook server without a token or password for local development






flowchart TD
    A[Dockerfile] --> B[Jupyter Image]
    B --> C[Container Starts]
    C --> D[Notebook Server on Port 8888]
    D --> E[Open in Browser]








Build the Jupyter Image
docker build -t my-jupyter-server .



Run the Jupyter Container
docker run -p 8888:8888 my-jupyter-server
Then open:
http://localhost:8888

Jupyter Notebook Service in Docker Compose
A Jupyter Notebook server can also be added as one of the services in docker-compose.yml.

services:
  notebook:
    image: jupyter/base-notebook:latest
    container_name: notebook
    ports:
      - "8888:8888"
    volumes:
      - ./notebooks:/home/jovyan/work
    working_dir: /home/jovyan/work
    command: start-notebook.sh --NotebookApp.token='' --NotebookApp.password=''


What happens in this Compose example?
This file defines a notebook service that:

starts a Jupyter Notebook server
maps port 8888 to your local machine
mounts the local ./notebooks folder into the container
allows you to edit notebooks locally while running them inside Docker






flowchart LR
    A[Local notebooks folder] --> B[Jupyter Container]
    B --> C[Notebook Server :8888]
    C --> D[Browser]









Example 4 | Jupyter with PostgreSQL in Docker Compose
A practical setup for exploring a data product’s data is to run Jupyter together with PostgreSQL.

  notebook:

title: Introduction to Docker
text:
Understanding Volumes
A volume is a way to store data outside the container itself.
This is important because containers are usually ephemeral. If a container is removed, its internal data can disappear. Volumes solve this by keeping the data in persistent storage managed by Docker.





flowchart LR
    A[Container] --> B[Writes Data]
    B --> C[Docker Volume]
    C --> D[Data Persists Even if Container is Removed]







Why do we need volumes?
Without a volume:

files created inside the container may be lost when the container stops or is deleted
database data may disappear
notebook work may not be saved outside the container

With a volume:

data survives container restarts
data can be reused by new containers
local folders can be connected to containers for live development



Two common volume patterns
There are two common ways to use volumes in Docker Compose:

named volumes
bind mounts



Named Volumes
A named volume is managed by Docker.
Example:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  postgres_data:
In this example:

postgres_data is the Docker-managed volume name
/var/lib/postgresql/data is the folder inside the PostgreSQL container where database files are stored

This means PostgreSQL writes its data into postgres_data, so even if the container is removed and recreated, the database files can still remain.





flowchart TD
    A[PostgreSQL Container] --> B["/var/lib/postgresql/data"]
    B --> C[Named Volume: postgres_data]
    C --> D[Persistent Database Files]








Bind Mounts
A bind mount connects a local folder on your machine to a folder inside the container.
Example:
services:
  notebook:
    image: jupyter/base-notebook:latest
    volumes:
      - ./notebooks:/home/jovyan/work
In this example:

./notebooks is the folder on your machine
/home/jovyan/work is the folder inside the container

This means:

files created in Jupyter appear in your local notebooks folder
if you edit files locally, the container sees those changes too






flowchart LR
    A[Local Folder ./notebooks] <--> B[Jupyter Container]
    B --> C["/home/jovyan/work"]








Volume syntax
The general syntax is:
volumes:
  - source:target
Where:

source can be a named volume or a local folder
target is the path inside the container



Example | PostgreSQL Volume
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: project_db
      POSTGRES_USER: postgres
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  postgres_data:
Why this matters:

PostgreSQL stores its internal files in /var/lib/postgresql/data
if we do not attach a volume, database data may be lost
with the volume, the data is persistent



Example: Jupyter Notebook Volume
services:
  notebook:
    image: jupyter/base-notebook:latest
    ports:
      - "8888:8888"
    volumes:
      - ./notebooks:/home/jovyan/work
    working_dir: /home/jovyan/work
    command: start-notebook.sh --NotebookApp.token='' --NotebookApp.password=''
Why this matters:

notebooks created in the container are saved in the local ./notebooks folder
the work is easier to version-control with Git
the files remain available even if the container is rebuilt



Example: Frontend Source Code Volume
During development, we sometimes mount the application folder into the container:
services:
  frontend:
    build: ./app/front
    ports:
      - "8501:8501"
    volumes:
      - ./app/front:/app
This means:

your local source code is linked to /app inside the container
code changes on your machine become visible inside the container
this is useful for faster development







Important



PAY ATTENTION TO THE PATHS




Named Volume vs Bind Mount
A simple rule of thumb:

use named volumes for databases and persistent service data
use bind mounts for source code, notebooks, and local development files



What happens if we remove a container?
If a container is deleted:

data stored only inside the container is lost
data stored in a volume can remain

That is why volumes are especially important for:

PostgreSQL
Jupyter notebooks
uploaded files
model artifacts
logs



Check existing volumes
You can list Docker volumes with:
docker volume ls
Inspect a specific volume with:
docker volume inspect postgres_data
Remove an unused volume with:
docker volume rm postgres_data


Why volumes matter for a data product
When building a data product, volumes can be used for:

PostgreSQL data persistence
Jupyter notebook development
possible shared data folders
saving files even when containers are rebuilt







Important



Without volumes, removing or recreating containers can cause important data to be lost.

text:
What Is an ORM?
An Object-Relational Mapper (ORM) connects Python objects to relational database records. We describe a table using a Python class and work with instances of that class. SQLAlchemy translates those operations into SQL when the session executes them.








Python / SQLAlchemy
PostgreSQL idea
Product example




Model class
Table
Carousel → carousels


Object instance
Row
One carousel named Summer offers


Column(...)
Column and its database type
name stored as a string


primary_key=True
Unique row identifier
A carousel’s UUID id


ForeignKey(...)
Reference to another table
An alternative’s carousel_id


relationship(...)
Python navigation between related objects
carousel.alternatives


Session
Coordinates queries and a transaction
Add changes, then commit or roll back








flowchart LR
    accTitle: How an ORM connects Python code to SQL rows
    accDescr: Python model objects are passed to a SQLAlchemy session. SQLAlchemy uses its engine and database driver to send SQL to PostgreSQL, and returns rows as model objects.
    O["Python objects<br/>Carousel, Alternative"] <-->|"add or query"| S["SQLAlchemy Session"]
    S <-->|"execute SQL"| E["Engine + driver"]
    E <-->|"SQL / rows"| D[("PostgreSQL tables")]






Read the arrows in both directions. Creating an object only creates a Python value. Adding it to a session schedules persistence. A flush sends pending SQL; committing makes the transaction durable. A query can load records back into Python objects. See SQLAlchemy’s ORM quick start.

API Schemas and ORM Models Have Different Jobs
The repository uses Pydantic schemas in app/backend/db/schemas.py to describe API inputs and outputs. It uses SQLAlchemy models in app/backend/db/models.py to describe stored records. A validated request still needs application code to create an ORM object and save it.





flowchart LR
    accTitle: API validation and database persistence are separate steps
    accDescr: JSON input is validated by a Pydantic request schema. Endpoint code creates a SQLAlchemy object, and a session writes that object to a database row.
    J["JSON request"] --> P["Pydantic schema<br/>Validate input"]
    P --> F["Endpoint code<br/>Apply product rules"]
    F --> O["SQLAlchemy model<br/>Describe a stored object"]
    O --> D[("Database row<br/>Saved through a session")]






Read the arrows as a conversion: input data becomes a validated Python value, then a persistent object, then a row. Defining a Pydantic BaseModel alone does not create a SQL table.

title: Database | PostgreSQL
text:
The Product’s Actual SQLAlchemy Models
The following code is copied from app/backend/db/models.py. Base comes from app/backend/db/database.py, where the backend creates its engine and session factory.
from sqlalchemy import Column, Integer, String, DateTime, ForeignKey, JSON
from sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql import UUID
from sqlalchemy.orm import relationship
import uuid
from datetime import datetime

from .database import Base

class Carousel(Base):
    __tablename__ = "carousels"

    id = Column(UUID(as_uuid=True), primary_key=True, default=uuid.uuid4)
    name = Column(String, nullable=False)
    total_alternatives = Column(Integer, nullable=False)
    visible_count = Column(Integer, nullable=False)
    created_at = Column(DateTime, default=datetime.utcnow)
    round_number = Column(Integer, default=1)

    alternatives = relationship("Alternative", back_populates="carousel", cascade="all, delete-orphan")
    interactions = relationship("Interaction", back_populates="carousel", cascade="all, delete-orphan")

class Alternative(Base):
    __tablename__ = "alternatives"

    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True, index=True)
    carousel_id = Column(UUID(as_uuid=True), ForeignKey("carousels.id"), nullable=False)
    alt_id = Column(Integer, nullable=False)  # Position within carousel
    title = Column(String, nullable=False)
    alpha = Column(Integer, default=1)
    beta = Column(Integer, default=1)
    impressions = Column(Integer, default=0)
    clicks = Column(Integer, default=0)

    carousel = relationship("Carousel", back_populates="alternatives")

class Interaction(Base):
    __tablename__ = "interactions"

    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True, index=True)
    carousel_id = Column(UUID(as_uuid=True), ForeignKey("carousels.id"), nullable=False)
    round = Column(Integer, nullable=False)
    timestamp = Column(DateTime, default=datetime.utcnow)
    displayed = Column(JSON, nullable=False)  # List of alt_ids displayed
    clicked = Column(Integer, nullable=True)  # alt_id clicked, or None
    reward = Column(Integer, nullable=False)  # 0 or 1

    carousel = relationship("Carousel", back_populates="interactions")

Carousel: the Parent Record

__tablename__ = "carousels" chooses the SQL table name.
id is a UUID primary key. default=uuid.uuid4 asks SQLAlchemy to generate a fresh identifier during insertion; passing the function lets it run for each new record.
nullable=False requires values for the name and size settings.
created_at and round_number have Python-side insert defaults.
alternatives and interactions let us navigate from a carousel object to its children.



Alternative: an Option Belonging to One Carousel
There are two identifiers with different jobs:







Field
Meaning




id
The unique primary key of the row across the entire alternatives table.


alt_id
The option’s local label within a carousel, such as 1, 2, or 3.


carousel_id
The UUID of the parent carousel.



alpha and beta store the Beta distribution parameters; impressions and clicks store counts. In this backend version these are integer counts. A Python relationship such as alternative.carousel loads or refers to the parent object.


Interaction: What Happened in One Round

displayed is JSON holding local alternative IDs, such as [1, 3].
clicked holds the local ID selected by the user, or None for no click.
reward records the outcome, conventionally 0 or 1.
round and timestamp tell us when the event occurred.

clicked is currently a plain integer, not a foreign key. The models also do not define database checks for valid visible counts or rewards. Those rules need explicit application validation and/or additional database constraints; field names and comments alone do not enforce them.


Foreign Key vs. Python Relationship





erDiagram
    CAROUSELS ||--o{ ALTERNATIVES : contains
    CAROUSELS ||--o{ INTERACTIONS : records
    CAROUSELS {
        UUID id PK
        string name
        int round_number
    }
    ALTERNATIVES {
        int id PK
        UUID carousel_id FK
        int alt_id
    }
    INTERACTIONS {
        int id PK
        UUID carousel_id FK
        json displayed
        int clicked
    }






Read one → many: one carousel can have many alternatives and interactions. ForeignKey("carousels.id") creates a database constraint on a column. relationship(...) provides Python object navigation and does not add another SQL column. back_populates connects the two directions.
The parent relationships use cascade="all, delete-orphan". Through the ORM, children follow the parent’s lifecycle, and removing a child from the parent’s collection can mark it for deletion. This is different from a database ON DELETE CASCADE constraint, which is not declared on these backend foreign keys. See relationship patterns and ORM cascades.


What SQL Does This Mapping Describe?
The following PostgreSQL DDL is compiled from the actual model metadata. It describes the tables; SQLAlchemy also creates indexes declared with index=True.
CREATE TABLE carousels (
    id UUID NOT NULL,
    name VARCHAR NOT NULL,
    total_alternatives INTEGER NOT NULL,
    visible_count INTEGER NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP WITHOUT TIME ZONE,
    round_number INTEGER,
    PRIMARY KEY (id)
);

CREATE TABLE alternatives (
    id SERIAL NOT NULL,
    carousel_id UUID NOT NULL,
    alt_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
    title VARCHAR NOT NULL,
    alpha INTEGER,
    beta INTEGER,
    impressions INTEGER,
    clicks INTEGER,
    PRIMARY KEY (id),
    FOREIGN KEY(carousel_id) REFERENCES carousels (id)
);

CREATE TABLE interactions (
    id SERIAL NOT NULL,
    carousel_id UUID NOT NULL,
    round INTEGER NOT NULL,
    timestamp TIMESTAMP WITHOUT TIME ZONE,
    displayed JSON NOT NULL,
    clicked INTEGER,
    reward INTEGER NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (id),
    FOREIGN KEY(carousel_id) REFERENCES carousels (id)
);
Notice that default=1 and default=datetime.utcnow do not appear as SQL DEFAULT clauses. They are supplied by SQLAlchemy when it inserts a record. A server_default is a separate setting used when PostgreSQL itself should supply a value, including for direct SQL inserts. See column defaults.


Create Tables, Then Work with Records
This is the table-creation pattern used in app/backend/main.py:
from .db import models
from .db.database import engine

models.Base.metadata.create_all(bind=engine)
Importing models registers the tables with Base.metadata. The engine knows how to connect to PostgreSQL. create_all() checks for missing tables and creates them; use a migration tool when an existing schema must change. See SQLAlchemy metadata and schema creation.


Save a Carousel and Its Alternatives
The next example is written for a Python session launched from app/, with the backend dependencies installed and DATABASE_URL set to a database using the backend schema.
from backend.db.database import SessionLocal
from backend.db.models import Carousel, Alternative

with SessionLocal() as session:
    carousel = Carousel(
        name="Summer offers",
        total_alternatives=2,
        visible_count=1,
    )
    carousel.alternatives = [
        Alternative(alt_id=1, title="Free delivery"),
        Alternative(alt_id=2, title="Discount"),
    ]
    session.add(carousel)
    try:
        session.commit()
    except Exception:
        session.rollback()
        raise
    session.refresh(carousel)
    print(carousel.name, carousel.round_number, len(carousel.alternatives))
Expected output:
Summer offers 1 2
The relationship supplies the children’s carousel_id when the parent and children are inserted. commit() flushes the inserts and commits the transaction. refresh() reloads the parent record. Closing the session releases its database resources.





flowchart TD
    accTitle: A database transaction has a success and a failure path
    accDescr: Create Python objects, add them to a session, and try to commit. On success the records are saved. On failure roll back the transaction and report the error. Close the session in either case.
    O["Create Python objects"] --> A["session.add"]
    A --> C["session.commit<br/>Flush SQL and commit transaction"]
    C -->|"success"| S["Records saved"]
    C -->|"failure"| R["session.rollback<br/>Discard uncommitted changes"]
    S --> X["Close session"]
    R --> X






The example saves the parent and children in one transaction. Compare this with app/backend/db/crud.py, whose current creation function commits the parent first and the alternatives in a second transaction. Grouping dependent changes in one transaction is a useful improvement when they should succeed together. See session and transaction basics.


Read the Same Records with SQL and the ORM
from sqlalchemy import select
from backend.db.database import SessionLocal
from backend.db.models import Carousel

with SessionLocal() as session:
    names = session.scalars(
        select(Carousel.name).where(Carousel.name == "Summer offers")
    ).all()
    print(names)
After the insert above, expect ['Summer offers'] in a fresh practice database. The corresponding SQL query is:
SELECT name FROM carousels WHERE name = 'Summer offers';

text:
Normalized ETL Design: A Separate Exercise
The following four-table design belongs to app/etl/Database/models.py. It stores displayed alternatives in individual rows rather than the backend’s JSON list. Its integer carousel IDs and table names differ from the backend model version above.



Normalized ETL schema



Normalized Schema in SQL
This is a SQL illustration of the normalized ETL design. It includes additional CHECK rules; matching ORM models would need explicit CheckConstraint declarations to create those rules.
CREATE TABLE carousels (
    carousel_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    total_alternatives INT NOT NULL CHECK (total_alternatives > 0),
    visible_count INT NOT NULL CHECK (visible_count > 0),
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    is_active BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE
);

CREATE TABLE alternatives (
    alt_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    carousel_id INT NOT NULL REFERENCES carousels(carousel_id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    title VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    alpha FLOAT NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    beta FLOAT NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    impressions INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    clicks INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE TABLE interaction_events (
    event_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    carousel_id INT NOT NULL REFERENCES carousels(carousel_id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    round_number INT NOT NULL,
    clicked_alt_id INT NULL REFERENCES alternatives(alt_id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
    reward INT NOT NULL CHECK (reward IN (0, 1)),
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE TABLE event_displayed_alternatives (
    event_id INT NOT NULL REFERENCES interaction_events(event_id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    alt_id INT NOT NULL REFERENCES alternatives(alt_id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    slot_position INT NOT NULL,
    was_clicked BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE,
    PRIMARY KEY (event_id, alt_id)
);


Reading the Normalized Design
Use this schema for the ETL modeling exercise; the current backend uses the separate model mapping above.


carousels
Stores the main carousel project settings.
Columns:

carousel_id — unique identifier
name — project name
total_alternatives — total number of bandits in the project
visible_count — how many alternatives are shown each round
created_at — creation timestamp
is_active — whether the carousel is active


alternatives
Stores all bandit alternatives for a given carousel.
Columns:

alt_id — unique alternative identifier
carousel_id — parent carousel
title — alternative label
alpha — Beta prior/posterior alpha parameter
beta — Beta prior/posterior beta parameter
impressions — number of times shown
clicks — number of clicks
created_at — creation timestamp



interaction_events
Stores one row per interaction round.
Columns:

event_id — unique interaction event
carousel_id — associated carousel
round_number — round index
clicked_alt_id — clicked alternative, if any
reward — 1 for click, 0 for no click
created_at — interaction timestamp



event_displayed_alternatives
Stores which alternatives were displayed in an event.
Columns:

event_id — parent event
alt_id — displayed alternative
slot_position — position in the visible carousel
was_clicked — whether that displayed alternative received the click

This table is important because it lets us reconstruct: - what was shown, - in what order, - and which alternative was selected



SQLAlchemy Models for the Normalized ETL Design

│   ├── data/

Database/database.py
Configuring the Database
"""
Database Configuration
"""

import os
from pathlib import Path
from dotenv import load_dotenv

from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker, declarative_base


# --------------------------------------------------
# Load environment variables
# --------------------------------------------------
load_dotenv(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2] / ".env")


# --------------------------------------------------
# Build DATABASE URL
# --------------------------------------------------
def _build_database_url() -> str:
    database_url = os.environ.get("DATABASE_URL")
    if database_url:
        return database_url

    db_user = os.environ.get("DB_USER")
    db_password = os.environ.get("DB_PASSWORD")
    db_name = os.environ.get("DB_NAME")
    db_host = os.environ.get("DB_HOST", "db")       # Docker default
    db_port = os.environ.get("DB_PORT", "5432")

    if db_user and db_password and db_name:
        return f"postgresql+psycopg2://{db_user}:{db_password}@{db_host}:{db_port}/{db_name}"

    raise RuntimeError(
        "DATABASE_URL is not set and DB_USER/DB_PASSWORD/DB_NAME are incomplete."
    )


DATABASE_URL = _build_database_url()


# --------------------------------------------------
# Engine
# --------------------------------------------------
engine = create_engine(
    DATABASE_URL,
    pool_pre_ping=True,   # avoids stale connections (important in Docker)
    echo=False            #? set True for debugging
)


# --------------------------------------------------
# Base class for models
# --------------------------------------------------
Base = declarative_base()


# --------------------------------------------------
# Session
# --------------------------------------------------
SessionLocal = sessionmaker(
    autocommit=False,
    autoflush=False,
    bind=engine
)


# --------------------------------------------------
# FastAPI dependency
# --------------------------------------------------
def get_db():
    """
    Provides a database session per request
    """
    db = SessionLocal()
    try:
        yield db
    finally:
        db.close()


Database/models.py
from sqlalchemy import (
    Column,
    Integer,
    String,
    Boolean,
    Float,
    ForeignKey,
    DateTime
)
from sqlalchemy.sql import func
from sqlalchemy.orm import relationship
from Database.database import Base


"""
In your case:

Carousel = parent
Alternative = child

If an Alternative does not belong to any Carousel anymore, it becomes an orphan.
"""

class Carousel(Base):
    __tablename__ = "carousels"

    carousel_id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True, autoincrement=True)
    name = Column(String(255), nullable=False)
    total_alternatives = Column(Integer, nullable=False)
    visible_count = Column(Integer, nullable=False)
    created_at = Column(DateTime(timezone=True), server_default=func.now())
    is_active = Column(Boolean, default=True)

    alternatives = relationship(
        "Alternative",
        back_populates="carousel",
        cascade="all, delete-orphan" #
    )
    events = relationship(
        "InteractionEvent",
        back_populates="carousel",
        cascade="all, delete-orphan"
    )


class Alternative(Base):
    __tablename__ = "alternatives"

    alt_id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True, autoincrement=True)
    carousel_id = Column(
        Integer,
        ForeignKey("carousels.carousel_id", ondelete="CASCADE"),
        nullable=False
    )
    title = Column(String(255), nullable=False)
    alpha = Column(Float, default=1, nullable=False)
    beta = Column(Float, default=1, nullable=False)
    impressions = Column(Integer, default=0, nullable=False)
    clicks = Column(Integer, default=0, nullable=False)
    created_at = Column(DateTime(timezone=True), server_default=func.now())

    carousel = relationship("Carousel", back_populates="alternatives")


class InteractionEvent(Base):
    __tablename__ = "interaction_events"

    event_id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True, autoincrement=True)
    carousel_id = Column(
        Integer,
        ForeignKey("carousels.carousel_id", ondelete="CASCADE"),
        nullable=False
    )
    round_number = Column(Integer, nullable=False)
    clicked_alt_id = Column(
        Integer,
        ForeignKey("alternatives.alt_id", ondelete="SET NULL"),
        nullable=True
    )
